title: Is it a sin?
hook: tattoos, a drink, a bet: the questions people actually search, and Paul's way of thinking about them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord's Day, and your line: the first day, a new start. Christians differ on which day; Paul had a word for arguments like that.

Late at night, a search bar. Is it a sin to get a tattoo. To drink. To bet on the game. The questions people type are rarely about the creeds. They're about Saturday night, and skin, and money. Online answers come fast, certain, and contradictory. The first Christians had their own versions. Could you eat meat that had been offered to an idol? Did one holy day matter more than another? Paul got questions like these in letters, and his answer wasn't a list but a way of thinking. Today's word is its name.
screen: `A SEARCH BAR, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `TATTOOS, A DRINK, A BET.` → `PAUL GOT THESE QUESTIONS TOO.`

segments.voice: Adiaphora. Greek for things indifferent: not commanded, not forbidden. Stoic philosophers used the word, and in the 1500s Lutheran reformers made it a church word for matters left to conscience. The idea is Paul's. He tells the church in Rome to welcome one another, "but not to doubtful disputations," and on holy days he says, in the King James Bible: "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind." To another church: "All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient." Allowed isn't the same as helpful. Where the line falls, churches honestly differ. Tattoos: an old law of Moses says, "nor print any marks upon you." Many Christians read it as part of ancient Israel's mourning and worship laws; some avoid tattoos because of it. Coptic Christians in Egypt have long tattooed a small cross on the wrist. Alcohol: Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding, and a letter of Paul's says, "be not drunk with wine." Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and Anglicans use wine at communion; many Baptist, Pentecostal and Methodist churches have asked members not to drink, and serve grape juice. Gambling: the Bible never names it. The United Methodist Church opposes it; the Catholic catechism says games of chance aren't wrong in themselves, but become wrong when they take what someone needs. Sex and dating are a bigger conversation, and a later one. Under all of it, Paul adds a rule about the other person: "judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way." Be persuaded. Then be kind to the person who lands somewhere else.
screen: `ADIAPHORA: THINGS INDIFFERENT.` · `FULLY PERSUADED IN HIS OWN MIND.` · `TATTOOS, WINE, A BET.` · `NO STUMBLINGBLOCK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one is-it-a-sin question you've carried, about yourself or someone you love. Don't answer it; just notice how it sits in your body: tight, guilty, curious, annoyed. Then picture someone you respect who lands on the other side of it. If you pray, ask for a clear conscience and a kind heart; if you don't, let the question rest without a verdict.
Adiaphora: things indifferent, matters left to conscience, where sincere Christians land in different places.
Your line: be persuaded, and be kind. Allowed isn't always helpful. Day one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Christians usually take questions like tattoos, drinking or gambling to their church's teaching, their pastor or priest, and their own conscience. Churches answer them differently, and many point to Paul's advice in Romans 14 not to judge one another over disputed matters.

original.note: Greek: things indifferent, neither commanded nor forbidden. the Lutheran reformers' word for matters left to conscience.

trapdoor: what you thought: every is-it-a-sin question has one yes-or-no answer.
what it means: some things the Bible commands or forbids, and some it leaves to conscience. churches draw that line in different places.
what a scholar hears: adiaphora began as a Stoic term; Lutherans argued over it in the adiaphorist controversy after 1548, and the Formula of Concord (1577) takes it up in article ten.
recall: a shout of praise that began as save

notes: Rewritten 2026-10-06 from the five-year map; confirm with the Keeper. Replaced 'Made for you (Mark 2:27)'. Why: 'is it a sin?' searches (tattoos, alcohol, gambling) are the audience's most-searched questions and had no home; the old lesson repeated day 166 (Lord of the sabbath, Mark 2:23–28), which teaches the same grain-field story and the same line 'the sabbath was made for man'. Day 166 now carries that teaching alone.

No verdicts given: each topic states who says what. Confirm fairness: Coptic wrist-cross tattoo custom; Catholic/Orthodox/Lutheran/Anglican wine at communion vs many Baptist, Pentecostal and Methodist churches asking members to abstain and serving grape juice; UMC opposition to gambling; CCC 2413 paraphrase.
Sex and dating deliberately left for a later, careful lesson (one line only).
'Adiaphora' history: Stoic origin; the Lutheran adiaphorist controversy (Leipzig Interim, 1548); Formula of Concord Article X. Confirm.
